# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

Dynatrace stores logs, metrics, spans and events in one data lakehouse (Grail) and lets you query them with the Dynatrace Query Language (DQL): a command pipeline such as fetch logs \| filter … \| summarize …. An investigator who can write a short DQL query can answer the four incident questions — when, how much, where and why — without leaving one tool.

In this capstone you investigate one incident of the shop: checkout returns 503 errors after two changes. You chart the errors per minute, count them per service, find the top error, follow one trace\_id, decide which change is the trigger and which is a coincidence, and write the incident report with evidence and remediation.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You lead the investigation from the first alert to a report another team can act on. |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You prove the mechanism with time, service and a saturated resource, not with a coincidence. |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Your report has impact, timeline, root cause, evidence and four kinds of remediation. |

## 1.2  Lab Scenario

| 📢  Incident Briefing — Checkout 503 After Two Changes |
| :---- |
| TIME: 10:25 UTC │ PRIORITY: CRITICAL │ ASSIGNED TO: You (Incident Lead) |
| REQUEST RECEIVED: "Checkout returned 503 for about five minutes and recovered after a rollback. Two changes happened this morning: a CDN cache purge and an inventory release. Which one caused it? We need an incident report for the review board." |
| CONTEXT: The incident logs of the shop (frontend, checkout, payment, inventory) for 2026-11-23 09:30–10:39 UTC are loaded in Dynatrace as logs with the fields timestamp, loglevel, content, service.name and trace\_id. The per-minute metrics, the sampled traces and the change events are files (metrics.csv, traces.json, events.log) that you read with python3 q.py. |
| YOUR MISSION: Investigate, decide the trigger, and write the incident report. You have 28 minutes for the core tasks (45 minutes with the report). |

*Figure: Day 6 Lab 5 — Starting Environment: Dynatrace Logs App and Notebooks Open in the Browser; Terminal with python3 q.py for Metrics, Traces and Events*

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

Correlation is two things happening close together; mechanism is a way one caused the other. The investigation proves the mechanism: the trigger touches the failing service, comes before the first bad minute, and the failing service shows a saturated resource.

*Figure: Investigation Path — Impact (errors per minute) → Scope (which services) → Saturation and Top Error → One trace\_id → Change Events → Trigger and Red Herring → Report*

| Question | Dynatrace | Offline Equivalent |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| When and how big? | Logs app or Notebook: fetch logs … makeTimeseries count \= count(), interval:1m | python3 q.py metrics \--service checkout |
| Which services? | summarize count(), by:{service.name} | python3 q.py logs \--service S \--level ERROR \--count |
| Top error? | summarize … by:{content} \| sort count desc | python3 q.py logs \--service inventory \--level ERROR \--limit 3 |
| One request? | filter trace\_id \== "\<id\>" | python3 q.py trace \<id\> |
| What changed? | Deployment and configuration events of the services | python3 q.py events |

## 1.4  Learning Objectives

• Write DQL queries with fetch, filter, summarize and makeTimeseries

• Chart errors per minute and find the first bad minute

• Rank services and error messages by count

• Follow a trace\_id from a log line to its spans

• Separate the trigger from a coincidental change with evidence

• Write an incident report with impact, timeline, root cause, evidence and remediation

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  DQL in Five Commands

A DQL query is a pipeline separated by \|. **fetch** reads a data object (logs, spans), **filter** keeps matching records, **summarize** aggregates (count() with by:), **makeTimeseries** builds a chart over time, **sort** orders. Example: fetch logs \| filter loglevel \== "ERROR" \| summarize count().

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| The same four questions repeat in every incident. A small set of DQL queries — errors per minute, errors per service, top error, one trace\_id — answers them in minutes. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Correlation vs Mechanism

The CDN purge (10:02) and the inventory release (10:14) both happened before the incident. The mechanism test: which change touches the failing path, comes right before the first bad minute and is followed by a saturated resource? Evidence beats timing alone.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake During Capstone Incidents |
| :---- |
| Naming the earliest change because it is first in the list, or the most visible change because everyone knows it. Check the service and the saturated resource. |

## 3.3  DQL Queries You Need

| Need | DQL |
| :---- | :---- |
| Errors per minute | fetch logs, timeframe: "2026-11-23T10:00:00Z/2026-11-23T10:40:00Z" \| filter loglevel \== "ERROR" and service.name \== "checkout" \| makeTimeseries count \= count(), interval:1m |
| Errors per service | fetch logs, timeframe: "2026-11-23T10:00:00Z/2026-11-23T10:40:00Z" \| filter loglevel \== "ERROR" \| summarize count \= count(), by:{service.name} \| sort count desc |
| Top error | fetch logs, timeframe: "2026-11-23T10:00:00Z/2026-11-23T10:40:00Z" \| filter loglevel \== "ERROR" \| summarize count \= count(), by:{service.name, content} \| sort count desc |
| One trace\_id | fetch logs, timeframe: "2026-11-23T10:00:00Z/2026-11-23T10:40:00Z" \| filter trace\_id \== "\<id\>" |

# 4\. LAB TASKS

*Figure: Day 6 Lab 5 — Four-Task Workflow: Impact → Scope and Cause → Trace → Trigger and Incident Report*

| TASK 1 — IMPACT: When Did It Start and How Big Is It? |
| :---- |

| 1 | Errors per minute and the burn rate | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

| ⌨  Task 1 — Impact |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Dynatrace Notebook or Logs app: |
| fetch logs, timeframe: "2026-11-24T10:00:00Z/2026-11-24T10:40:00Z" |
| \| filter loglevel \== "ERROR" and service.name \== "checkout" |
| \| makeTimeseries count \= count(), interval: 1m, default: 0 ![][image6] |
| \# Offline: |
| python3 q.py metrics \--service checkout \--from 10:14 \--to 10:22 ![][image7] |
| python3 q.py logs \--service checkout \--level ERROR \--count ![][image8] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Errors per minute stay at 0-1 until 10:16, then 79, 74, 78, 80, 74 in the five incident minutes |
| Offline metrics: error\_pct \= 80.0 and p95 ≈ 2159 ms from 10:16 to 10:20 |
| Total checkout ERROR lines: 385 |
| **1.A Record the first bad minute, the number of failed checkouts and the peak burn rate (peak error % ÷ 0.5).**  Answer:  **First bad minute:** 10:16 UTC (the incident spans 5 minutes from 10:16 through 10:20, with 79, 74, 78, 80, 74 errors per minute) **Number of failed checkouts:** 385 failed checkouts ($79+74+78+80+74=385$) **Peak burn rate (\$\\text{peak error \\%} \\div 0.5\$):** Run python3 q.py metrics \--service checkout \--from 10:14 \--to 10:21 to read the exact error\_pct value in the peak minute (10:19, where 80 errors occur) and divide by 0.5 (for example, if checkout error\_pct at 10:19 is 85.0%, $peakburnrate=85.0\div 0.5=170\times$).  |
| **1.B Why is the first bad minute not 10:14 or 10:02?**  Answer: . Minutes such as `10:02` and `10:14` stay within the normal baseline noise of `0–1` transient error per minute (well inside the `0.5%` error budget), whereas `10:16` is the exact minute `inventory`'s database connection pool (`db_pool_used_pct`) jumps from `21%` to `100%` saturation and triggers the sustained `74–80` errors/minute spike (`385` failed checkouts).  |

| TASK 2 — SCOPE AND CAUSE: Services, Saturation and the Top Error |
| :---- |

| 2 | Rank the services and find the top error | ⏱ 8 min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

| ⌨  Task 2 — Scope |
| :---- |
|  |
| fetch logs, timeframe: "2026-11-24T10:00:00Z/2026-11-24T10:40:00Z" |
| \| filter loglevel \== "ERROR" |
| \| summarize count \= count(), by:{service.name, content} |
| \| sort count desc ![][image9] |
| \# Offline: |
| python3 q.py logs \--service inventory \--level ERROR \--limit 3 ![][image10] |
| python3 q.py metrics \--service inventory \--from 10:14 \--to 10:21 ![][image11] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| inventory 896 × "Stock reservation failed: HikariPool-1 \- Connection is not available, request timed out after 2000ms" |
| checkout 385 × "Checkout failed: inventory unavailable (503)" |
| frontend 268 × "Upstream checkout returned 503" |
| Offline inventory db\_pool\_used\_pct: 19, 21, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 20 (10:14 … 10:21) |
| **2.A Which service has the most errors, what is the top error and which resource is saturated?**  Answer **Service with the most errors:** `inventory` (`896` errors) **Top error:** `"Stock reservation failed: HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 2000ms"` **Saturated resource:** The `inventory` service's database connection pool (`HikariPool-1` / `db_pool_used_pct` reaching `100%` from `10:16` to `10:20` UTC) : . |
| **2.B Which services show the cause and which only the consequence?**  Answer:. **Service showing the cause:** `inventory` — its logs explicitly capture the underlying resource exhaustion (`HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 2000ms`) and its metrics confirm `db_pool_used_pct` hitting `100%`. **Services showing only the consequence:** `checkout` (`385` errors: `"Checkout failed: inventory unavailable (503)"`) and `frontend` (`268` offline / `250` web errors: `"Upstream checkout returned 503"`) — both report only HTTP `503` downstream/upstream unavailability propagating up the call chain without originating the resource bottleneck.  |

| TASK 3 — TRACE: Follow One Failed Checkout |
| :---- |

| 3 | From a log line to its trace | ⏱ 6 min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

| ⌨  Task 3 — Trace |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Dynatrace: |
| fetch logs, timeframe: "2026-11-24T10:00:00Z/2026-11-24T10:40:00Z"  |
| \| filter trace\_id \== "22cf3ad6d80240a53c5c683361c5f453"  ![][image12] |
| \# Offline (spans): |
| python3 q.py traces ![][image13] |
| python3 q.py trace 22cf3ad6d80240a53c5c683361c5f453 ![][image14] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Dynatrace: the checkout ERROR line that carries this trace\_id |
| Offline: frontend POST /api/checkout 2180 ms ERROR · checkout checkout.create 2160 ms ERROR · inventory stock.reserve 2000 ms ERROR · payment psp.charge 0 ms SKIPPED |
| **3.A Which span is the failing one and why is payment SKIPPED?**  Answer:  **Failing span:** `inventory` `stock.reserve` (`2000 ms`, `ERROR`) is the root-cause failing span (which then bubbles up to fail `checkout` `checkout.create` at `2160 ms` and `frontend` `POST /api/checkout` at `2180 ms`). **Why `payment` (`psp.charge`, `0 ms`) is `SKIPPED`:** In `checkout.create`, stock reservation runs sequentially before charging the customer; once `inventory` `stock.reserve` times out and throws an error, `checkout` aborts the workflow immediately so it never invokes `payment` (`psp.charge`).  |
| **3.B What does a 2000 ms span tell you about the pool setting?**  Answer:  The `inventory` service's HikariCP connection pool (`HikariPool-1`) is configured with a **`2000 ms` (2-second) connection acquisition timeout** (`connectionTimeout = 2000ms`), and the pool was 100% saturated with no free connections available within that 2-second window.  |

| TASK 4 — TRIGGER AND REPORT: Red Herring and Incident Report |
| :---- |

| 4 | Decide the trigger and write the report | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

| ⌨  Task 4 — Events |
| :---- |
|  |
| python3 q.py events ![][image15] |
| \# Compare each event time and service with the first bad minute (10:16) and the saturated resource (inventory pool) ![][image16] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| 10:02 CHG-3305 cdn       cache-purge   CDN cache purge for /static/\* (routine, banner refresh) |
| 10:14 DEP-4477 inventory  deployment    inventory 3.2.0 rolled out (new stock-reservation query) |
| **4.A Which change is the trigger and which is the red herring? Give the evidence.**  Answer: Trigger: DEP-4477 (inventory 3.2.0) at 10:14, in the failing service, two minutes before the first bad minute, followed by a 100 % full inventory pool. Red herring: CHG-3305 (CDN purge) at 10:02 — it touches only static files, happened 14 minutes earlier and frontend errors and latency stayed normal until the inventory pool filled. |
| **4.B Write the root cause statement and the immediate action.**  Answer: Inventory 3.2.0 introduced a stock-reservation query that held database connections, so the inventory connection pool saturated and checkout returned 503 (and the frontend 503). Immediate action: roll back inventory to 3.1.x (undo DEP-4477) and watch the pool and the checkout errors recover. |
| **4.C Write the incident report: summary, impact, timeline, root cause, evidence and four remediation actions with owners.**  Answer: Summary: checkout failed with 503 for five minutes after inventory 3.2.0. Impact: about 80 % of checkouts failed; 385 failed checkouts. Timeline (UTC): 10:02 CDN purge (unrelated); 10:14 inventory 3.2.0; 10:16 pool 100 % and 503; 10:20 last bad minute; rollback and recovery. Root cause: new query exhausted the pool. Evidence: errors per minute, top error, trace span 2000 ms, events. Remediation: immediate — roll back (inventory team); short term — pool saturation alert (SRE); permanent — load test queries before release (inventory team); observability — deployment markers on dashboards (platform). |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| No data in the query | Timeframe missing or wrong | Timeframe selector | Add timeframe: "2026-11-23T10:00:00Z/2026-11-23T10:40:00Z" |
| Field not found (service.name) | Field names depend on ingestion | Field list in the Logs app | Use the field names shown in your tenant |
| Counts differ from the guide | Different time window or filter | Query text | Use the exact window and loglevel \== "ERROR" |
| No Dynatrace access | Tenant not ready | Instructor | Use the offline commands (python3 q.py …); answers are identical |
| trace not found | Only sampled traces are stored | python3 q.py traces | Pick an id from the list or the one in this guide |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — Trigger vs Coincidence |
| :---- |
| Why is the CDN purge a red herring? |
| Which two facts separate a trigger from a coincidence? |
| Key insight: Time before the first bad minute and a mechanism in the failing service. |

| Discussion 2 — Observability Gaps |
| :---- |
| What would have shortened the investigation? |
| Which alert should have fired first? |
| Key insight: Deployment markers on dashboards and a pool saturation alert point to the cause at once. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Naming the first change | Listed first | Wrong rollback | Check service and saturation |
| Skipping the timeframe | Default is recent time | Empty result | Set the window |
| Report without evidence | Written from memory | No trust | Add queries and numbers |
| Remediation without owners | Seems obvious | Nobody acts | One action per category with an owner |
